title: When Large Language Models Meet Law: Dual-Lens Taxonomy, Technical Advances, and Ethical Governance

bias_targets.methodology: Reviewing existing empirical literature (e.g., Vats et al.) that applies LLMs to Supreme Court cases to uncover biases in statutory and outcome prediction outputs.
Reviewing existing empirical literature that applies LLMs to judicial cases to identify religious disparities and biases in the generated model outputs.

Reviewing studies (e.g., Blodgett et al.) that evaluate the performance and accuracy of NLP tools in processing specific demographic dialects, such as African American English (AAE), compared to standard English.

Reviewing theoretical frameworks and classification systems (e.g., Weidinger et al., Bommasani et al.) that examine how language models exacerbate social inequality, reinforce stereotypes, and propagate latent flaws into downstream legal applications.

Surveying technical optimizations in the literature (e.g., Cuconasu et al.) aimed at mitigating positional bias within Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems used for legal information retrieval.
